new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is non-contrastive and falls on the penultimate mora (moraic count: a long vowel = two moras, so maˈnoo-type words stress the first half of a final long vowel, cf. the author's Takuu analysis). Regular exceptions involve vowel sequences: in ao, ae, ea sequences the second vowel does not count as a separate stress-bearing mora (paona [ˈpaona], haeko [ˈhaeko], maea [ˈmaya]), and prevocalic high vowels become glides (uila [ˈwila]), shifting stress leftwards; hakaˈkii ~ haˈkkii shows the same rule surviving vowel syncope.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned for Nukeria. For the closely related Takuu the same author (2014: 4) states secondary stress on every second mora to the left of the primary stress; not asserted for Nukeria.
new_statements.exceptions: 'Some regular exceptions' illustrated by paona [ˈpaona] 'place-name', maea [ˈmaya] 'rope', haeko [ˈhaeko] '(v.) hate', haraoa [haˈrawa] 'bread, flour' and glide formation of i/u before stressed vowels (uila [ˈwila]); the rule is otherwise stated without qualification.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, phonetic citation forms in IPA collected in 2013 fieldwork on Puhuria; phrase-level examples ([tee ˈtama ~ ˈttama] 'the person') show the definite article unstressed. Stress described as non-phonemic.
new_statements.identity_note: Davletshin's consultants insist the language is 'Nukeria'; 'Nukuria' is the name in the regional Polynesian 'trade language' (Davletshin 2014: 3 fn. 1; 2018: 115). Same variety as Glottolog nuku1259 (Nukuria/Nuguria/Fead), documented on Puhuria islet in 2013. Caveat on the older statement: Davletshin (2014: 14 fn. 7; 2018: 118) argues that the Nuguria data of Thilenius 1902 (and the German South-Sea Expedition) were collected from a Luangiua/Ontong Java (onto1237) immigrant and 'cannot be considered Nukeria', so Thilenius's 1902 p. 84 footnote that stress 'does not differ from Samoan' may not describe Nukeria proper.
